objectives: Distinguish mutex vs RWLock vs spinlock.

slides.title: Locks, the working menu
slides.body:
**Mutex** (`pthread_mutex_t`, `std::mutex`): mutual exclusion. One holder at a time; others block. Fair-ish; supports priority inheritance to avoid priority inversion. Cost: ~25ns to acquire when uncontended; ~100ns + context switch when contended (~µs total).

**RWLock** (`pthread_rwlock_t`, `std::shared_mutex`): allows many readers OR one writer. Useful when reads vastly outnumber writes. Cost: more state to manage; slower than mutex in the uncontended case. Win when reads dominate AND lock-hold time is meaningful.

**Spinlock**: busy-wait instead of blocking. Useful when lock-hold time is < context-switch time (~1µs). Used inside the kernel + in lock-free algorithms. Burns CPU while waiting — use sparingly.

**Recursive mutex**: same thread can lock it multiple times (must unlock same # times). Convenient but a code smell — usually means your invariants are unclear.

**Reader-writer-lock vs RCU**: RCU (Read-Copy-Update) is even faster than RWLock for read-heavy workloads. Readers don't take any lock; writers copy + atomically swap. Used pervasively in the Linux kernel.

slides.title: Futex: the Linux fast-path
slides.body:
**futex** (Fast Userspace Mutex): Linux's primitive that mutexes are built on. Two ops:
- `futex_wait(addr, val)`: if `*addr == val`, sleep. Else return immediately.
- `futex_wake(addr, N)`: wake up to N waiters on `addr`.

The magic: futex_wait + futex_wake are kernel calls, but the FAST PATH (uncontended lock) is pure userspace atomic operations. Only when contention exists does the kernel get involved.

Uncontended mutex acquire:
1. CAS (compare-and-swap) on the lock word in userspace.
2. CAS succeeds → done. No syscall.

Contended mutex acquire:
1. CAS fails.
2. `futex_wait()` syscall to sleep.
3. When holder releases: CAS to 0 + futex_wake() to wake one waiter.

The glibc + Rust + Java synchronization primitives all use this pattern. The lock cost on Linux: ~25ns uncontended (just the CAS), ~1µs contended (syscall + context switch).

slides.title: Lock-free vs wait-free
slides.body:
**Lock-free**: at any time, *some* thread makes progress. No locks; uses atomic operations (CAS, fetch-add).

**Wait-free**: *every* thread makes progress in bounded steps. Strictly stronger than lock-free.

Classical lock-free queue (Michael-Scott 1996): linked list with atomic head + tail. Enqueue: CAS to append a node. Dequeue: CAS to advance head. Failed CAS → retry. Lock-free; some thread always succeeds; failed retries are bounded by other threads' success.

**ABA problem**: thread A reads value X, gets preempted. Thread B changes X → Y → X (same address, different version). A resumes with stale assumption that the value is X. CAS succeeds (because the bits match) but the world has changed. Mitigations: tagged pointers (version counter), hazard pointers (track which addresses are in use), generational counters.

Production lock-free: Disruptor (LMAX), JCTools, crossbeam (Rust), folly (Facebook). Production use is niche — most apps are fine with locks. Lock-free is for queues with millions-of-ops-per-second throughput where lock contention is the bottleneck. Wait-free is mostly academic.

question.question: Derive futex's fast-path cost
question.goal: Uncontended mutex lock + unlock. Cost in CPU cycles (rough)?

steps.prompt: Lock: CAS instruction (1 cycle uncontended) + atomic-fence overhead (~10 cycles on modern CPUs). Unlock: atomic store + fence. Total cycles?
hints: Atomic ops + fences are ~10-20 cycles each.
steps.reveal: ~20-50 cycles, ~10-20ns on a 3GHz CPU. No syscall.

steps.prompt: Contended lock: CAS fails + futex_wait syscall + context switch + later futex_wake + context switch. Cost?
steps.reveal: ~1µs — about 100× more than uncontended. Contention is the killer; reduce contention by sharding/finer locks.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Uncontended: ~20ns. Contended: ~1µs. Ratio: 50×.}}$$ Avoid lock contention. Sharded locks (per-thread, per-bucket) often eliminate contention entirely. Lock-free structures: alternative when sharding doesn't fit the data structure.

question.question: Lock-free CAS-based code is vulnerable to the ABA problem when:
options: Two threads compete for the same lock.
A value changes from X to Y to X between a read and a CAS — the CAS succeeds incorrectly because the bits match.
question.explanation: ABA: thread A reads X, gets preempted. Thread B does X → Y → X. Thread A resumes with stale 'world view' (assumes nothing changed since X). CAS succeeds because bits match. But underneath, something happened. Mitigations: tagged pointers (counter + pointer in one CAS word), hazard pointers, epoch-based reclamation.

hints: What's special about the pattern X → Y → X?
The CAS only checks bits, not the history.
slides.workedSolution: CAS checks the current value matches the expected; doesn't check the history. If the value cycled X → Y → X between read + CAS, the CAS succeeds but a different state was reached + unreached. Common in lock-free linked lists: node was freed, reused; old pointer in new node's place. Mitigations: version-tagged pointers (CAS on (ptr, version) together), hazard pointers, RCU's epoch-based reclamation.

question.question: CAS cost ~10ns. 10K threads contending on one CAS. Worst-case wait time per op (ms)?
Lock contention in production
question.prompt: Your service uses a single shared cache protected by a mutex. Under load, you see threads spending 80% of their time waiting for the lock. Walk through three approaches to reduce contention, ordered from least to most invasive.
Explain in two or three sentences why most production code uses regular mutexes instead of lock-free data structures.
question.rubric: Mentions that mutexes are simpler to reason about, easier to debug, and fast enough (~25ns uncontended); lock-free is correct only with careful design + tagged pointers + memory-ordering reasoning; the engineering cost outweighs the throughput gain except in genuinely-contended hot paths.
